claim: Circadian rhythms are daily cycles of most bodily processes driven by a system of intrinsic biological clocks organized in a complex hierarchical manner.
source: Circadian rhythms are daily cycles of most bodily processes driven by a system of intrinsic biological clocks organized in a complex hierarchical manner.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about circadian rhythms.

claim: The circadian system provides the organism with an evolutionary conserved advantage.
source: This mechanism ensures a temporal coordination of physiology and behavior with a near 24 hr period of rest-activity and feeding-fasting cycles, thus providing the organism with an evolutionary conserved advantage (Albrecht, 2012; Spoelstra et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albrecht, 2012 and Spoelstra et al., 2016.

claim: In mammals, the circadian system is driven by a central pacemaker situated in the paired suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the hypothalamus.
source: In mammals, the circadian system is driven by a central pacemaker, situated in the paired suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the hypothalamus, and by secondary oscillators located in peripheral organs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the mammalian circadian system.

claim: The SCN clock is readjusted on a daily basis mainly by light inputs coming from the retina.
source: The SCN clock is readjusted on a daily basis, mainly by light inputs coming from the retina.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SCN entrainment.

claim: The central pacemaker orchestrates peripheral clocks through a combination of neuronal, endocrine, and metabolic signaling pathways.
source: In turn, the central pacemaker orchestrates peripheral clocks through a combination of neuronal, endocrine, and metabolic signaling pathways (Saini et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saini et al., 2015.

claim: Metabolic processes in the liver, skeletal muscle, and other organs are subject to daily oscillations.
source: As a result, metabolic processes in the liver, skeletal muscle, and other organs are subject to daily oscillations (Asher and Sassone-Corsi, 2015) with the SCN keeping these rhythms in appropriate synchrony with each other.
evidence: Supported by citation to Asher and Sassone-Corsi, 2015.

claim: Skeletal muscle is responsible for ~70% of glucose uptake resulting from ingested carbohydrates.
source: Skeletal muscle is responsible for ~70% of glucose uptake resulting from ingested carbohydrates (DeFronzo et al., 1981; Gachon et al., 2017), and perturbations in glucose sensing and metabolism in this organ are strongly associated with insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Muoio and Newgard, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to DeFronzo et al., 1981 and Gachon et al., 2017.

claim: Perturbations in glucose sensing and metabolism in skeletal muscle are strongly associated with insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.
source: Skeletal muscle is responsible for ~70% of glucose uptake resulting from ingested carbohydrates (DeFronzo et al., 1981; Gachon et al., 2017), and perturbations in glucose sensing and metabolism in this organ are strongly associated with insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Muoio and Newgard, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muoio and Newgard, 2008.

claim: In rodents, the skeletal muscle clock plays an essential role in maintaining proper metabolic homeostasis.
source: In rodents, it has been established that the skeletal muscle clock plays an essential role in maintaining proper metabolic homeostasis, with skeletal muscle pathologies stemming from clock disruption via deletion of the core clock component Bmal1 (Andrews et al., 2010; Harfmann et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andrews et al., 2010 and Harfmann et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of muscle insulin sensitivity by modulating glucose uptake, with a reduction in Glut4 mRNA and protein levels, has been reported in two muscle-specific Bmal1 knockout models.
source: Disruption of muscle insulin sensitivity by modulating glucose uptake, with a reduction in Glut4 mRNA and protein levels, has been reported in two muscle-specific Bmal1 knockout (KO) models (Dyar et al., 2014; Harfmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dyar et al., 2014 and Harfmann et al., 2016.

claim: In humans, diurnal variations in glucose tolerance have been described.
source: In humans, diurnal variations in glucose tolerance have been described (Kalsbeek et al., 2014), although the molecular mechanism responsible for such variations remains largely unexplored.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kalsbeek et al., 2014.

claim: Feeding-fasting cycles accompanying rest-activity rhythms represent major timing cues in the synchronization of peripheral clocks, including skeletal muscle oscillators.
source: Feeding-fasting cycles accompanying rest-activity rhythms represent major timing cues in the synchronization of peripheral clocks, including skeletal muscle oscillators (Dibner and Schibler, 2015; Wehrens et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dibner and Schibler, 2015 and Wehrens et al., 2017.

claim: In murine models, 3.4% to 16% of the skeletal muscle transcriptome is expressed in a circadian manner.
source: Although several studies have reported that in murine models 3.4% to 16% of the skeletal muscle transcriptome is expressed in a circadian manner (McCarthy et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2007; Dyar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Hodge et al., 2015), it is unclear to what extent the muscle circadian transcriptome is regulated by feeding-fasting rhythms and additional central synchronizers, and how local muscle clocks contribute in generating these transcript oscillations.
evidence: Supported by citations to McCarthy et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2007; Dyar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Hodge et al., 2015.

claim: Cell-autonomous circadian clocks operating in human primary skeletal myotubes have been recently characterized.
source: Cell-autonomous circadian clocks operating in human primary skeletal myotubes (hSKM) established from muscle biopsies have been recently characterized (Perrin et al., 2015; Hansen et al., 2016; Loizides-Mangold et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Perrin et al., 2015; Hansen et al., 2016; Loizides-Mangold et al., 2016.

claim: Proper function of cellular oscillators in human skeletal myotubes is indispensable for the normal secretion of interleukin 6, interleukin-8, the monocyte chemotactic protein 1 and additional myokines.
source: Importantly, proper function of these cellular oscillators is indispensable for the normal secretion of interleukin 6 (IL-6), interleukin-8 (IL-8), the monocyte chemotactic protein 1 (MCP-1) and additional myokines, regulating skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity and inflammation (Perrin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perrin et al., 2015.

claim: 5748 rhythmic genes were identified at the pre-mRNA or/and mRNA level with a False Discovery Rate of 5% in human skeletal muscle biopsies.
source: This method allowed for the identification of 5748 rhythmic genes that were rhythmic at the pre-mRNA or/and mRNA level with a False Discovery Rate (FDR) of 5% (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis from human skeletal muscle biopsies.

claim: 4792 genes showed rhythmic transcription at the intronic pre-mRNA level in human skeletal muscle.
source: When rhythmicity levels were further analyzed, it became apparent that 4792 genes showed rhythmic transcription at the intronic pre-mRNA level (Figure 1A, upper and middle left panels).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis from human skeletal muscle biopsies.

claim: Only 57% of rhythmic pre-mRNA transcripts were also rhythmic at the mRNA level.
source: However, from these rhythmic pre-mRNA transcripts, only 57% were also rhythmic at the mRNA level (R-I.R-E, upper panels Figure 1A), likely because of the longer half-life of their mRNA.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis from human skeletal muscle biopsies.

claim: Among rhythmic pre-mRNA transcripts, those that are only rhythmic at the pre-mRNA level have a longer half-life compared to those that are rhythmic at the mRNA level.
source: Indeed, approximation of mRNA half-life by the exon/intron ratio showed that among these rhythmic pre-mRNA transcripts, those that are only rhythmic at the pre-mRNAs level (R-I) have a longer half-life compared to those that are rhythmic at the mRNA level (R-E and R-I.R-E, Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on analysis of exon/intron ratio from RNA-seq data, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Around 10% of the quantified transcriptome (956 genes) were only rhythmic at the mRNA level.
source: In parallel, around 10% of the quantified transcriptome (956 genes) were only rhythmic at the mRNA level (R-E, Figure 1A, lower panels), likely through post-transcriptional regulation and in particular mRNA degradation (LuckLück et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis from human skeletal muscle biopsies, with inference about mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Among genes rhythmic at the pre-mRNA level, those with higher amplitude of transcription had a greater probability to be rhythmic at the mRNA accumulation level.
source: Amplitude distribution suggested that among the genes that were rhythmic at the pre-mRNA level, those with higher amplitude of transcription had a greater probability to be rhythmic at the mRNA accumulation level (R-I.R-E, Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on amplitude distribution analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rhythmic gene transcription in human skeletal muscle was distributed into two phases of transcript accumulation at 04:00 and 16:00.
source: As previously reported in mice, rhythmic gene transcription was distributed into two phases of transcript accumulation (04:00 and 16:00, Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on phase distribution analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The afternoon peak (16:00) was enriched in genes related to muscle contraction and mitochondrial activity.
source: The afternoon peak (16:00) was enriched in genes related to muscle contraction and mitochondrial activity (Figure 1—source data 2), whereas homologous genes in rodents were shared between the active but also the resting phase (McCarthy et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2007; Hodge et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on gene ontology analysis of rhythmic genes, with comparison to rodent studies supported by citations.

claim: Among genes highly activated in the middle of the night (04:00), many were associated with inflammation and immune response.
source: In contrast, among the genes highly activated in the middle of the night (04:00), many were associated with inflammation and immune response (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Core clock genes ARNTL (BMAL1), NPAS2, CLOCK, PER2, PER3, CRY2, NR1D1 (REV-ERBα) and RORA showed high amplitude oscillations in human skeletal muscle.
source: Among the rhythmic genes, we observed high amplitude oscillations for the core clock genes ARNTL (BMAL1), NPAS2, CLOCK, PER2, PER3, CRY2, NR1D1 (REV-ERBα) and RORA, which were well synchronized among the 10 individuals (Figure 1G).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: TFEB, KLF13, KLF15, PPARD, and MYOD1 showed oscillatory profiles in human skeletal muscle.
source: In addition, several transcription factors associated with muscle metabolism and physiology like TFEB, a key regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy that also regulates glucose homeostasis and oxidative phosphorylation (Mansueto et al., 2017), KLF13, which plays a role in cardiac muscle cell development (LavalleeLavallée et al., 2006), and KLF15, an important transcriptional regulator of muscle lipid metabolism (Haldar et al., 2012), showed an oscillatory profile. Moreover, also PPARD, the most abundant PPAR isoform in skeletal muscle and master regulator of muscle mitochondrial function (Jordan et al., 2017), and MYOD1, the key regulator of myogenesis and direct target of BMAL/CLOCK (Andrews et al., 2010) were rhythmically expressed in human skeletal muscle, likely orchestrating the temporal muscle transcriptome (Figure 1H).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1H, with functional context supported by citations.

claim: The 16:00 peak is enriched in MEF2 and MYOD1 motifs, in phase with MYOD1 expression.
source: As shown in Figure 1I, the 16:00 peak is enriched in MEF2 and MYOD1 motifs, in phase with MYOD1 expression, and both proteins synergize to activate gene expression (Taylor and Hughes, 2017).
evidence: Based on DNA-binding motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1I, with functional context supported by citation.

claim: The 4:00 peak is enriched in MYC and AP1 families of transcription factors.
source: In parallel, the 4:00 peak is enriched in MYC and AP1 families of transcription factors, both downstream of the MAP kinase pathway activated by exercise (Aronson et al., 1997) or wound-induced inflammation (Aronson et al., 1998).
evidence: Based on DNA-binding motif enrichment analysis, with functional context supported by citations.

claim: CLOCK expression was reduced by at least 80% upon siCLOCK depletion in human skeletal myotubes.
source: CLOCK expression was reduced by at least 80% upon siCLOCK depletion, as assessed by RNA-seq and quantitative real-time PCR (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The circadian amplitude of Bmal1-luciferase bioluminescence reporter profile became dampened upon siCLOCK compared to siControl and non-transfected counterparts.
source: As expected, the circadian amplitude of Bmal1-luciferase bioluminescence reporter profile became dampened upon siCLOCK compared to siControl and non-transfected counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Based on bioluminescence recording data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Out of 16,776 mapped genes, 1330 genes (8%) were significantly altered in siCLOCK-transfected hSKM compared to controls.
source: Out of the 16,776 mapped genes, the median values for all the time points, reflecting the overall expression levels of 1330 genes (8%), were significantly altered in siCLOCK-transfected hSKM compared to their control counterparts, with 742 being downregulated and 588 being upregulated (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Core clock genes NR1D1 (REVERBα), NR1D2 (REVERBβ), PER3, TEF, BHLHE41 (DEC2), and DBP were significantly downregulated upon CLOCK depletion.
source: As expected, core clock gene expression was affected, with NR1D1 (REVERBα), NR1D2 (REVERBβ), PER3, TEF, BHLHE41 (DEC2), and DBP being significantly downregulated, and CRY1 being upregulated upon CLOCK depletion (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CRY1 was upregulated upon CLOCK depletion.
source: As expected, core clock gene expression was affected, with NR1D1 (REVERBα), NR1D2 (REVERBβ), PER3, TEF, BHLHE41 (DEC2), and DBP being significantly downregulated, and CRY1 being upregulated upon CLOCK depletion (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Genes encoding for proteins essential for vesicle formation including SNAREs, solute transporters, and Rab GTPases exhibited significantly altered expression levels upon CLOCK depletion.
source: Remarkably, genes encoding for proteins essential for vesicle formation including SNAREs, solute transporters, and Rab GTPases exhibited significantly altered expression levels upon CLOCK depletion (Supplementary file 1-table S2).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 42 transcripts involved in lipid metabolism were affected by CLOCK disruption.
source: In addition, 42 transcripts involved in lipid metabolism were affected by CLOCK disruption. These comprised genes related to glycerophospholipid and triglyceride metabolism as well as lipid storage and transport (Figure 2C), in addition to those regulating inositol phosphate (Figure 2D) and sphingolipid metabolic pathways (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: Total phosphatidylcholine levels were downregulated in the absence of a functional myotube clock.
source: Importantly, the observed modifications in gene expression level were in an accord with significant alterations in absolute lipid metabolite levels, resulting in total phosphatidylcholine levels being downregulated, and glycosylceramide levels being upregulated in the absence of a functional myotube clock (Figure 2F, Supplementary file 1-table S1, donors 7–10 for in vitro part).
evidence: Based on lipidomics analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Glycosylceramide levels were upregulated in the absence of a functional myotube clock.
source: Importantly, the observed modifications in gene expression level were in an accord with significant alterations in absolute lipid metabolite levels, resulting in total phosphatidylcholine levels being downregulated, and glycosylceramide levels being upregulated in the absence of a functional myotube clock (Figure 2F, Supplementary file 1-table S1, donors 7–10 for in vitro part).
evidence: Based on lipidomics analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Genes involved in insulin-stimulated and contraction-induced glucose uptake, comprising TBC1D13, TBC1D4 (AS160), 14-3-3θ (YWHAQ), RAB35, STX6, and PDPK1 (PDK1), were significantly downregulated upon siCLOCK.
source: Our differential analysis in human muscle cells demonstrates that genes involved in insulin-stimulated and contraction-induced glucose uptake, comprising TBC1D13, TBC1D4 (AS160), 14-3-3θ (YWHAQ), RAB35, STX6, and PDPK1 (PDK1), were significantly downregulated upon siCLOCK (Supplementary file 1-table S2), highlighting the pleiotropic effect of the skeletal muscle CLOCK gene/protein in regulating glucose uptake in response to insulin and/or to contraction.
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: CLOCK mRNA was reduced by siCLOCK by 91 ± 2% as determined by RT-qPCR.
source: Matching the changes observed by RNA-seq, CLOCK mRNA was reduced by siCLOCK as determined by RT-qPCR (Figure 3A), leading to a reduction in CLOCK protein expression by 74% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CLOCK protein expression was reduced by 74% upon siCLOCK treatment.
source: Matching the changes observed by RNA-seq, CLOCK mRNA was reduced by siCLOCK as determined by RT-qPCR (Figure 3A), leading to a reduction in CLOCK protein expression by 74% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The expression of the 14-3-3θ protein was decreased by about 28% upon siCLOCK treatment.
source: Moreover, the expression of the 14-3-3θ protein, a key regulator of GLUT4 translocation (Sakamoto and Holman, 2008; Kleppe et al., 2011), was decreased by about 28% under these conditions (Figure 3C), matching the decrease in its gene expression (Supplementary File 1-table S2).
evidence: Based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C, with functional context supported by citations.

claim: Basal glucose uptake was significantly reduced by 31 ± 3% in siCLOCK-transfected myotubes compared to siControl counterparts.
source: Importantly, we observed a significant decrease in both basal (30%), and insulin-stimulated (27%) glucose uptake in siCLOCK-transfected myotubes, as compared to their siControl counterparts (Figure 3D left and right panels, respectively).
evidence: Based on glucose uptake assay shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake was significantly reduced by 28 ± 3% in siCLOCK-transfected myotubes compared to siControl counterparts.
source: Importantly, we observed a significant decrease in both basal (30%), and insulin-stimulated (27%) glucose uptake in siCLOCK-transfected myotubes, as compared to their siControl counterparts (Figure 3D left and right panels, respectively).
evidence: Based on glucose uptake assay shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 994 rhythmic genes (7.65% of the global transcriptome) were identified in synchronized human skeletal myotubes.
source: Briefly, after conversion of the raw data to log2 RPKM values and filtering for log2 RPKM >0, temporal patterns of the resulting 12,985 genes were grouped into 16 models (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source datas 1 and 2), with models 1 to 15 comprising 994 rhythmic genes (7.65%), and model 16 comprising 11,991 non-rhythmic genes (92.35%).
evidence: Based on rhythmic analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Model 1 comprises 73 genes classified as rhythmic in both donors upon siControl and siCLOCK.
source: According to our analysis, model 1 comprises 73 genes, classified as rhythmic in both donors upon siControl and siCLOCK, models 2 and 3 include 39 and 34 genes, respectively, that are rhythmic in both siControl donors and in one siCLOCK donor respectively, and model 4 comprises 44 genes that are rhythmic in siControl, but not in siCLOCK (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on rhythmic analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Models 2 and 3 include 39 and 34 genes, respectively, that are rhythmic in both siControl donors and in one siCLOCK donor respectively.
source: According to our analysis, model 1 comprises 73 genes, classified as rhythmic in both donors upon siControl and siCLOCK, models 2 and 3 include 39 and 34 genes, respectively, that are rhythmic in both siControl donors and in one siCLOCK donor respectively, and model 4 comprises 44 genes that are rhythmic in siControl, but not in siCLOCK (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on rhythmic analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Model 4 comprises 44 genes that are rhythmic in siControl, but not in siCLOCK.
source: According to our analysis, model 1 comprises 73 genes, classified as rhythmic in both donors upon siControl and siCLOCK, models 2 and 3 include 39 and 34 genes, respectively, that are rhythmic in both siControl donors and in one siCLOCK donor respectively, and model 4 comprises 44 genes that are rhythmic in siControl, but not in siCLOCK (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on rhythmic analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Circadian core clock genes exhibited a rhythmic mRNA profile in siControl and a flattened, but still rhythmic, profile upon siCLOCK.
source: Circadian core clock genes clustered to model 1, as they exhibited a rhythmic mRNA profile in siControl and a flattened, but still rhythmic, profile upon siCLOCK (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating a presence of partially functional circadian oscillator.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 190 genes were qualified as rhythmic in the two analyzed cell cultures and were clustered into models 1–4.
source: In summary, 190 genes were qualified as rhythmic in the two analyzed cell cultures, and were clustered into models 1–4 (Figure 4—source datas 1 and 2), as exemplified in Figure 4D (upper panels) and in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.
evidence: Based on rhythmic analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Among the 190 transcripts identified as rhythmic in hSKM cells, 99 were expressed in human muscle biopsies.
source: Among the remaining 133 genes, 99 were expressed in human muscle biopsies. Within this group of overlapping genes, 35 were also qualified as rhythmic at the mRNA level (q-val <0.05) in muscle tissue (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Based on comparison of in vitro and in vivo RNA-seq datasets.

claim: 35 genes were qualified as rhythmic at the mRNA level in both human skeletal myotubes and muscle tissue.
source: Among the remaining 133 genes, 99 were expressed in human muscle biopsies. Within this group of overlapping genes, 35 were also qualified as rhythmic at the mRNA level (q-val <0.05) in muscle tissue (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Based on comparison of in vitro and in vivo RNA-seq datasets.

claim: Genes rhythmic in both in vivo and in vitro datasets were enriched at the 04:00 time point.
source: The genes rhythmic in both in vivo and in vitro datasets included the core clock components (Figure 5A), as well as functional genes that were enriched at the 04:00 time point (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on phase distribution analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genes implicated in glucose homeostasis (KLF11, GFPT2, NAMPT) and in muscle regeneration (PLAU, PLD1, PIM1) were rhythmic both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Interestingly, genes implicated in glucose homeostasis (KLF11, GFPT2, NAMPT) and in muscle regeneration (PLAU, PLD1, PIM1), were rhythmic both in vivo and in vitro, suggesting an important role for the circadian clock in regulating muscle physiology (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CLOCK depletion in cultured primary skeletal myotubes led to significant changes in gene expression.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that CLOCK depletion in cultured primary skeletal myotubes led to significant changes in gene expression (Figure 2), and related physiological outputs, comprising the regulation of basal and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, lipid homeostasis (Figure 3), and myokine secretion, as summarized in Figure 6.
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: More extensive rhythmic transcription was observed in human skeletal muscle compared to in vitro cell culture.
source: More extensive rhythmic transcription was observed in human skeletal muscle compared to in vitro cell culture as a large part of the in vivo mRNA rhythmicity was lost in vitro.
evidence: Based on comparison of in vivo and in vitro RNA-seq datasets.

claim: siRNA-mediated clock disruption in primary myotubes significantly affected the expression of ~8% of all genes.
source: siRNA-mediated clock disruption in primary myotubes significantly affected the expression of ~8% of all genes, with impact on glucose homeostasis and lipid metabolism.
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Genes involved in GLUT4 expression, translocation and recycling were negatively affected by CLOCK depletion.
source: Genes involved in GLUT4 expression, translocation and recycling were negatively affected, whereas lipid metabolic genes were altered to promote activation of lipid utilization.
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Lipid metabolic genes were altered to promote activation of lipid utilization upon CLOCK depletion.
source: Genes involved in GLUT4 expression, translocation and recycling were negatively affected, whereas lipid metabolic genes were altered to promote activation of lipid utilization.
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The circadian clock has an essential role for the circadian coordination of skeletal muscle glucose homeostasis and lipid metabolism in humans.
source: Our findings suggest an essential role for the circadian coordination of skeletal muscle glucose homeostasis and lipid metabolism in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A phase shift of 8–10 hr was observed between peripheral clocks in human and rodent skeletal muscle.
source: When comparing the circadian phases of core-clock components in our database to the temporal profiles of the corresponding genes in rodents (Dyar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014), we observed a phase shift of 8–10 hr. This result is in good agreement with a phase shift observed between peripheral clocks in nocturnal versus diurnal species, which is indeed typically smaller than 12 hr (Mure et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on comparison of human and rodent RNA-seq datasets, with context supported by citation to Mure et al., 2018.

claim: 107 common rhythmic genes were found between mouse and human skeletal muscle.
source: A comparison of our in vivo dataset (exonic signals) to published temporal gene expression databases of mouse skeletal muscle (Dyar et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014) revealed 107 common rhythmic genes between mouse and human skeletal muscle.
evidence: Based on comparison of human and mouse RNA-seq datasets, with citations to mouse studies.

claim: Among the 190 genes rhythmic in human skeletal myotubes, 30 were also rhythmic in U2OS cells.
source: Comparison of our in vitro dataset to the results published on U2OS cells (Hughes et al., 2009; Krishnaiah et al., 2017) revealed that among the 190 genes that were rhythmic in human skeletal myotubes, 30 were also rhythmic in U2OS.
evidence: Based on comparison with published U2OS cell data, supported by citations.

claim: TRIM47 exhibited rhythmic expression in human skeletal myotubes, in human muscle biopsies, and in U2OS cells.
source: Interestingly, the RING finger domain protein-encoding gene TRIM47 exhibited a rhythmic expression in human skeletal myotubes, in human muscle biopsies, and in U2OS cells.
evidence: Based on comparison of multiple RNA-seq datasets.

claim: Clock disruption induces a global switch in the genetic program towards slow type I muscle fibers.
source: Taken together these observations reinforce the hypothesis that clock disruption induces a global switch in the genetic program towards slow type I muscle fibers, as it was previously suggested in muscle-specific Bmal1 KO mice (Hodge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data, supported by citation to Hodge et al., 2015.

claim: The enzyme PI4K2A was downregulated at the mRNA level upon siCLOCK treatment.
source: Specifically, the enzyme PI4K2A, catalyzing the phosphorylation of phosphatidylinositol (PI) to phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P), was downregulated at the mRNA level, which may result in decreased PIP2 and PIP3 levels (Pullen et al., 1998; Sakamoto and Holman, 2008).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis, with functional context supported by citations.

claim: siCLOCK-depleted cells overexpressed MAPKAP1 (mSIN1), one component of the mTORC2 complex required for AKT phosphorylation.
source: Additionally, siCLOCK-depleted cells overexpressed MAPKAP1 (mSIN1), one component of the mTORC2 complex required for AKT phosphorylation (Frias et al., 2006), and CAV-3, essential for PI3K and AKT activity as well as GLUT4 translocation in muscle (Fecchi et al., 2006; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis, with functional context supported by citations.

claim: CAV-3 was overexpressed in siCLOCK-depleted cells.
source: Additionally, siCLOCK-depleted cells overexpressed MAPKAP1 (mSIN1), one component of the mTORC2 complex required for AKT phosphorylation (Frias et al., 2006), and CAV-3, essential for PI3K and AKT activity as well as GLUT4 translocation in muscle (Fecchi et al., 2006; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis, with functional context supported by citations.

claim: Both VAMP3 and STX6 were downregulated at the mRNA level upon clock disruption.
source: Both VAMP3 and STX6, which are involved in IL-6 secretion in mouse macrophages (Manderson et al., 2007), were downregulated at the mRNA level (Supplementary file 1-tables S2 and S6), confirming previous results that clock disruption impacts on vesicle trafficking and secretion (Marcheva et al., 2010; Saini et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis, with functional context supported by citations.

claim: Numerous genes involved in hormone secretion by pancreatic islets were affected in a similar manner in hSKM upon clock disruption as in clock disrupted human islets.
source: Importantly, when compared with results from clock disrupted human islets (Saini et al., 2016) we found that numerous genes involved in hormone secretion by pancreatic islets were affected in a similar manner in hSKM (Supplementary file 1-table S8).
evidence: Based on comparison with published data on human islets, supported by citation.

claim: An upregulation of CD36 and FABP3 was found upon clock disruption in hSKM.
source: Specifically, we found an increase in the long chain fatty acid transporter CD36 and in FABP3, consistent with previous results obtained in mouse skeletal muscle upon clock disruption (Hodge et al., 2015; Schiaffino et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis, with comparison to mouse studies supported by citations.

claim: An upregulation of MSTN was observed upon siCLOCK.
source: In addition, we observed an upregulation of MSTN upon siCLOCK, which could further promote the increase in CD36 and FABP3, leading to impaired glucose uptake (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The basal secretion of myokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1 exhibits a circadian pattern which was strongly disrupted in hSKM after CLOCK silencing in vitro.
source: We have previously demonstrated that the basal secretion of myokines, such as IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1, exhibits a circadian pattern, which was strongly disrupted in hSKM after CLOCK silencing in vitro (Perrin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perrin et al., 2015.

claim: Key regulators of the exocytosis machinery were altered upon clock disruption.
source: Here, our transcriptional analysis showed that key regulators of the exocytosis machinery were altered upon clock disruption (Supplementary file 1-tables S2 and S3).
evidence: Based on differential gene expression analysis.
